consensus_summary: Righteousness primarily denotes right standing before God (often as Christ's righteousness imputed/credited by faith) together with conformity to God's moral character and standard, frequently symbolized by a clean/white garment or robe; ethical conduct, infused transformation, covenant faithfulness, and social justice appear as common or minority alternatives.
book_summary: Righteousness is the doing of God's commandments—the law kept and worn as the garment of righteous acts—not a vague goodness nor a verdict only received.
consensus_core_identification: right standing before God (imputed gift by faith) and/or moral conformity to God's standard
book_core_identification: active keeping of God's commandments (the law kept) as the garment of righteous acts
boundary_disagreement: Book excludes pure forensic/imputed status ('verdict only received') and vague goodness, requiring actual commandment-keeping/righteous acts as constitutive; consensus treats the legal/relational status as primary or co-primary alongside ethical conformity.
material_contradiction: None of the core category (rightness/conformity to God); the book only rejects status-alone as definitional while preserving the shared moral-standard referent.
rationale: Minimum cores share the general category of rightness according to God's will/law, so the book does not replace the referent. It does, however, materially narrow the extension and boundary by elevating active law-keeping (garment of acts) and explicitly excluding a received verdict alone—the very element that dominates the consensus primary. This is refinement at the boundary (subset of cases), not contradiction of the central idea or novelty; ethical/behavioral senses already appear among the consensus alternatives.
strongest_objection: Pauline and mainstream Protestant usage centers righteousness on the forensic gift of right standing by faith apart from works of law (as the book itself notes is commonly taught), so the entry's exclusive emphasis on commandment-keeping risks legalism and under-weights justification.
